full_judgment:
Sikder Maqbul Huq J: This appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act-is directed against the order dated 13-1-1999, passed by Special Tribunal No. 1 Barguna, in Special Powers Case No. 10 of 1998, challenging framing of charge against the accused appellant under section 19(f) of the Arms Act. 

 4. The accused appellant filed an application for his discharge from the case but the learned Tribunal rejected the same without considering the facts and circumstances of the case and framed charge under section 19(f) of the Arms Act against him by the impugned order dated 13-1-1999. 

 7. Mr Kh. Mahbub Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the accused appellant, submits that according to the first information report and the seizure list a dagger 18" in length and one razor 8" in length were recovered from the possession of the accused appellant but a dagger or a razor does not come within the definition of arms as given in the Airs Act and, as such, it cannot be said that the accused appellant has committed an offence under section "19(f) of the Arms Act. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the accused appellant has referred to the case of Mozammel Hossain vs State, reported in 49 DLR 614, wherein it has been held that no license is required to keep possession of any dagger and, as such, a person does not commit an offence by keeping a dagger in his possession without any licence. 

 8. Mr Md lqbal Kabir, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the State, on the other hand, opposes the appeal and submits that one of the weapons recovered from the possession of the accused appellant is a dagger which has been enumerated in section 4 of the Arms Act, and a dagger as per this section is a weapon. If anybody keeps it without any licence he is liable to be punished under the aforesaid Act. In support of his argument he has referred to the case of Sha Din vs State reported in PLD 1961 (WP) Lahore 704, to the case of the State vs Amir Khan reported in PLD 1963 (WP) Peshawar 54; to the case of Maudud vs State reported in 1998 BLD 340 and also to the case of Shuinya @ Surju Ali vs State reported in 53 DLR 527. 

 9. The facts of the case reported in 49 DLR 614 are quite similar to the facts of the case before us. It has been held in the said case that no licence is required to keep a dagger and consequently, a person cannot be convicted if he is found in possession of a dagger. The aforesaid decision was given on consideration of Rule 30 of the Arms Act. Rule 30 of the Arms Rules 1924 is reproduced below for easy appreciation: 

 11. Now let us consider the decisions referred to by the learned Assistant Attorney-General. In PLD 1961 case, two unlicensed daggers were recovered from 2 accused persons one was 7" long and the other was 6" long and the defence case disclosed that these two arms welded offence by the accused and, as such, it was held that the accused should be convicted under section 19(f) of the arms Act for being in possession of the Arms without any licence. It has further been held that definition of arms as given in section 4 of the Arms Act is not exhaustive and no hard and fast rule can be laid down whether clasp knife would fall within the meaning of the word arms and determination of this question would depend on the circumstances of the case and not only the shape of the weapon or the size of its blade. If the weapon is obviously and primarily designed as an instrument for domestic use then it would normally fall outside the definition of arms, but if it is such that it cannot be described as an instrument of ordinary daily domestic use, and is, on the other hand, capable of being employed as a weapon of offence and defence, it would then be regarded as failing within the definition of arms. And if in a particular case, it is in fact, so employed, then it undoubtedly would fall within the definition of arms, The decision in the case reported in PLD 1963 page 54 is almost similar. It has been held in that case that a knife with blade 4½" long obviously and primarily was designed for being employed as a weapon of offence or defence. 

 13. It has been held in the case reported in 1998 BLD 340 that arms as defined in section 4 of the Arms Act includes a dagger, Rule 33 provides for obtaining licence for possession of such arms. It has further been held in this case that Rules being subordinate legislation made by the executive authority of the Government cannot override the provisions of the parent Act made by legislature and, as such, any Rule made in derogation of the provision of the parent Act must be held to be void. Since Rule 30 is not the appropriate Rule in this respect no question of its validity arises. It has been held in 53 DLR 527 that the main consideration for deciding whether a knife is an arm or not is to be decided on consideration of the fact as to for what purpose it is used or intended to be used. This decision has been given in the light of the decision given earlier in PLD 1961 and PLD 1963 cases. A dagger is included in the definition of arms under section 4 of the Arms Act but knife has not been described or enumerated therein. The case before us against the accused appellant is that a dagger was recovered from his possession and no knife was recovered. It may be mentioned that it is not only dagger but knife may also be treated as arm on consideration of the fact as to for what purpose it is used or intended to be used. 

 16. In the instant case, it appears from the record that the accused appellant along with other miscreants already entered into the house of one Asia Begum, wife of Abdul Majid Khan, village Latabaria PS and District Barguna for mischief and broke furniture of the house and then took away golden chain, cash money, etc by breaking open key of the almirah where after the local people caught hold of him with the incriminating weapons at the time of his retreat. The accused appellant kept the weapons with him and allegedly committed the offence as aforesaid. 

 Thus the accused appellant allegedly used the dagger as well as the razor as a weapon of offence. Thus we find a prima facie case against the accused appellant. The learned Tribunal committed no illegality in rejecting the application for discharging him from the case. In the result the appeal is dismissed. The stay order granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.
